note: Depiction-related actions against productions. Used to make licensing posture a cited fact rather than a model's impression, and to supply the Clearance Court with real precedent.

cases.name: Ringgold v. Black Entertainment Television
cases.fact_pattern: A poster of the artist's story quilt appeared in the background of a TV sitcom set, visible in nine segments totalling roughly 27 seconds.
cases.holding: Background use was not de minimis: the work was recognisable and displayed long enough for the audience to appreciate it.
cases.lesson: Recognisability plus duration defeats a de minimis defence for background artwork.

cases.name: Sandoval v. New Line Cinema
cases.fact_pattern: The photographer's transparencies appeared in the film Seven, out of focus, in shadow, and never in full.
cases.holding: De minimis: the works were not displayed with sufficient detail for the average observer to identify them.
cases.lesson: Out-of-focus, partial or fleeting artwork is defensible. Focus and framing decide the case, not mere presence.

cases.name: Gottlieb Development LLC v. Paramount Pictures
cases.fact_pattern: A pinball machine bearing the plaintiff's artwork appeared in the background of What Women Want for about three and a half minutes, never in focus.
cases.holding: De minimis in both copyright and trademark: the machine was always in the background and partly obscured.
cases.lesson: Duration alone does not defeat de minimis when the work is never the subject of the shot.

cases.name: Falkner v. General Motors
cases.fact_pattern: A Cadillac social campaign featured a photograph of a mural painted on a Detroit parking-garage elevator shed.
cases.holding: Court rejected GM's 17 U.S.C. §120(a) architectural defence: the mural was not part of an architectural work, so the panorama exception did not apply.
cases.lesson: Painted art on a building is NOT covered by the US architectural exemption. Murals are the single highest-value visual clearance risk.

cases.name: Williams (Revok) v. H&M
cases.fact_pattern: An H&M campaign was shot in front of a handball-court mural. H&M sued for a declaration that illegally-placed street art cannot be copyrighted.
cases.holding: H&M withdrew the action after public backlash; the artist's position prevailed.
cases.lesson: Illegality of placement is not a reliable defence to street-art copyright, and the reputational cost of arguing it is severe.

cases.name: Solid Oak Sketches v. 2K Games
cases.fact_pattern: Five tattoos inked on NBA players were reproduced on their in-game avatars.
cases.holding: Defence won on three independent grounds: de minimis, implied licence, and fair use.
cases.lesson: Tattoos on a real person the production is entitled to depict are usually defensible.

cases.name: Alexander v. Take-Two Interactive
cases.fact_pattern: Tattoos inked on wrestler Randy Orton were reproduced on his WWE 2K avatar.
cases.holding: Jury rejected fair use; the court rejected de minimis and implied licence. Damages awarded: $3,750.
cases.lesson: Tattoo claims are real but low-value. Worth flagging for a release, not worth a deep ownership investigation.

cases.name: Whitmill v. Warner Bros.
cases.fact_pattern: Mike Tyson's facial tattoo was replicated on another actor in The Hangover Part II.
cases.holding: Preliminary injunction denied but the court called the copyright claim strong; settled before trial.
cases.lesson: Replicating a tattoo onto a different person is materially riskier than filming the person who wears it.

cases.name: Rogers v. Grimaldi
cases.fact_pattern: Ginger Rogers objected to the film title Ginger and Fred.
cases.holding: Trademark yields to expressive works unless the use has no artistic relevance or explicitly misleads as to source.
cases.lesson: The controlling defence for brands appearing in narrative film. It is why most brand-owner suits against productions fail.

cases.name: Wham-O v. Paramount Pictures
cases.fact_pattern: A character was injured using a dry Slip 'N Slide; Wham-O alleged the depiction disparaged the product.
cases.holding: Injunction denied; the exaggerated depiction could not be read as endorsement or as a realistic safety claim.
cases.lesson: Brand-owner suits over depiction generally fail — but they are filed over UNFLATTERING depiction, which is the signal worth extracting.

cases.name: Caterpillar v. Walt Disney
cases.fact_pattern: Caterpillar bulldozers were depicted as instruments of villainy in George of the Jungle 2.
cases.holding: No infringement: viewers would not believe Caterpillar sponsored the film, and depicting a product is not use as a mark.
cases.lesson: Even villainous depiction of a branded product is usually lawful in the US.

cases.name: In-Sink-Erator / NBC 'Heroes'
cases.fact_pattern: A character's hand was mangled in a garbage disposal with the brand name visible; the manufacturer said the scene cast the product in an unsavoury light.
cases.holding: NBC digitally removed the trademark rather than litigate.
cases.lesson: Disparaging depiction is resolved by digital removal at post cost. Catching it before the lock is the entire value of a pre-flight scan.

cases.name: Louis Vuitton Malletier v. Warner Bros.
cases.fact_pattern: A character carried a counterfeit LV-style bag in The Hangover Part II and referred to it by name.
cases.holding: Dismissed under Rogers: artistically relevant and not explicitly misleading.
cases.lesson: Luxury houses do sue over film depiction even when the law favours the studio. Budget for defence, not just for licence.

cases.name: Bridgeport Music v. Dimension Films
cases.fact_pattern: A two-second, pitch-shifted guitar sample was used in a film soundtrack.
cases.holding: No de minimis defence for sound recordings in the Sixth Circuit: 'Get a licence or do not sample.'
cases.lesson: For recordings there is a live circuit split, so the safe assumption is that no amount of music is too short to clear.

cases.name: VMG Salsoul v. Ciccone
cases.fact_pattern: A 0.23-second horn sample was used in a Madonna recording.
cases.holding: De minimis DOES apply to sound recordings in the Ninth Circuit, expressly splitting with Bridgeport.
cases.lesson: Music exposure is jurisdiction-dependent within the US itself; the same cue can be clear in California and infringing in Ohio.

cases.name: NMPA v. Fullscreen
cases.fact_pattern: A YouTube multi-channel network monetised creator videos containing unlicensed compositions.
cases.holding: Settled with a licensing framework after the publishers' trade body sued the network rather than the creators.
cases.lesson: Music publishers enforce systematically and at platform scale. Music is the highest-frequency claim source for creators, not brands.

cases.name: Woods v. Universal City Studios
cases.fact_pattern: The interrogation-chair set in 12 Monkeys was built from an architect's drawing, 'Neomechanical Tower (Upper) Chamber'. The director admitted having seen the book.
cases.holding: Preliminary injunction GRANTED against distribution of the portions reproducing the drawing — while the film was already in theatres.
cases.lesson: The strongest case for pre-flight clearance: a background SET PIECE stopped a released studio film. Woods let distribution continue for a high six-figure settlement rather than enforce the order. Note the limit for detection — nothing in the frame identifies the chair as anyone's work, so this is derivative design, not a depicted work.

cases.name: Hart v. Warner Bros. (The Devil's Advocate)
cases.fact_pattern: A sculpted frieze in the film's set closely resembled Frederick Hart's 'Ex Nihilo' at Washington National Cathedral.
cases.holding: Settled; Warner Bros. digitally altered the sculpture for the home-video release.
cases.lesson: Remediation cost lands in post, after picture lock, and is paid per shot. Same limit as Woods: a derived set piece, not a depicted work.
